proves: The reverse direction, and the whole-name glossary hit. Transaction is claimed by both TXN and TRANS; the reverse index's tie-break takes the shorter token, which is the approved one.

Short words are kept whole, never clipped to look like abbreviations. FRAUD, RISK and SCORE are upper-cased and nothing more, and SCORE reports APPROVED with a null entry_id because the allow list, not a catalog row, is what permits it.

Longest match first. A strict word-by-word walk asks for Cross, gets nothing and emits CROSS_REFERENCE_ID; trying the longest run the reverse index knows reaches the multi-word catalog term, and the record shows the whole phrase as one token's word.

A placeholder term id from the TRM-9000xx block is attached. The glossary row records confidence 0.7 for it, but term_index carries only ids, so PhysicalName.confidence stays 1.0 - a gap between the field's docstring and what the index can supply, pinned here so it cannot change unnoticed.

A word the catalog has never abbreviated is upper-cased exactly as it stands - not shortened to ESCR, which would be inventing an abbreviation. The name's confidence drops to 0.0 because one word rests on nothing.
Half-abbreviated logical names are what schema exports actually contain. A word already written as a governed token in capitals is left alone rather than sent through the reverse index again.

The regression this rule exists for. Monthly is a candidate long form of MO, so without the already-governed check an approved MONTHLY would be rewritten to MO and a compliant name would silently change meaning.

append_class_word_when_missing adds the neutral class word when the rendered name ends in something that is not one, and only because this vocabulary governs VAL. Appending is the one edit this direction makes; nothing is removed to make room for it.
Date is claimed by the approved DT and the unapproved DTE. The tie-break takes the shorter token, so the reverse direction cannot emit an unapproved form for a word the standard has settled.

Number is claimed by NBR and NUM, which are the same length, so the length rule cannot decide and the lexicographic rule does. This is the one row in the corpus that needs the third tie-break, and it is the row that breaks first if the tie-break order changes.
The domain-pinned long form reverses to its own token. Account is claimed by ACCT and ACCNT and the shorter approved token wins, so a governed name never picks up the unapproved spelling.
